item.title: Ethics and Entrepreneurship: Foundations and Philosophical Perspectives
item.content:encoded:
Tina Dacin, Wilfrid Laurier University

Robin Holt, University of Bristol

Jean Clarke, Emlyon Business School

Jaco Lok, Macquarie University

Max Ganzin, Macquarie University

This Special Issue seeks to foreground the ethical dimensions of venture creation, opportunity recognition, and stakeholder engagement. It invites scholars to reimagine entrepreneurship as an inherently ethical practice, instead of viewing ethics as a constraint or an afterthought in the pursuit of economic gain. The intersection of ethics and entrepreneurship presents a unique opportunity to rethink and shape new ethical paradigms and foster innovative approaches to the persistent questions of responsibility, justice, and human flourishing. Entrepreneurship is often celebrated as a catalyst for creativity, imagination, and the capacity to disrupt, yet it has also drawn criticism for promoting ideals that valorize self-optimization and commodification. The foundational activities of entrepreneurship – venture creation, opportunity enactment, and creative destruction – are themselves inextricably bound to questions of ethics.

At the core of any entrepreneurial act is its willing encounter with, and encouragement of, 'the other' - whether this means novel products, new practices, uncertain futures, or transformed habits. From some philosophical perspectives, such as phenomenology, ethical experience also involves engagement with the 'other,' coupled with a refusal to confine or transform 'the other' to the norm. Yet this raises a critical question: if entrepreneurship courts 'the other,' does it then corrupt and empty this otherness in the calculated pursuit of economic returns? If ethics entails a life lived alongside difference, then how do entrepreneurial lives compare to those shaped and scripted by the certainty and commitment to principled forms of the good advocated by other philosophical positions, such as deontology? This SI is dedicated to papers investigating this uneasy yet intimate relationship between ethics and entrepreneurship.

Different philosophical perspectives can offer unique insights into the interplay between ethics and entrepreneurship, including virtue ethics, care ethics, pragmatism, capabilities approaches, as well as deontology and phenomenology. Similarly, different schools in entrepreneurship studies, from early traditions in evolutionary economics or trait theory, to more recent perspectives associated with alertness to opportunity, emergence and creativity, and actualization, provide different stimulus for ethicists. While entrepreneurship is often associated with opportunity-seeking and value creation, its concern with seeking support from others, and with growing an organizational form that sustains the livelihood of others, extends its modus operandi beyond economic and industrial narratives of profit, and product- and service innovation. Entrepreneurial ventures are embedded within complex networks of stakeholders, including employees, customers, investors, non-human systems, and communities. Navigating these relationships demands ethical judgment that balances competing interests, priorities, and values.

Unlike managerial decision-making, which tends to rely on established protocols, systems, and formalized structures, entrepreneurial judgment occurs in a context of greater uncertainty and fluidity, where ethical considerations are threaded into the very fabric of entrepreneurial practice. Entrepreneurs must establish trust, negotiate power dynamics, and create shared meaning among diverse stakeholders, all while remaining attuned to the broader societal and environmental implications of their actions. They continually navigate competing values, and face unpredictable consequences within 'spaces of ambiguity,' where loosened norms make ethical reasoning both precarious and generative. In such spaces, distinguishing a 'good reason' for action from simply 'a reason to act' carry significant personal, social and commercial resonance, raising fundamental questions about the nature of ethical responsibility in conditions of flux and uncertainty; about the requirement to follow rules or break them; about the intimacy between the social and ethical commitments inherent in entrepreneurship; and about the relationship between entrepreneurial flourishing and care.

If we can still speak of 'the entrepreneur,' it is as a figure that challenges the viability of the sovereign self, continually narrating identity through stories of venturing and novelty. The entrepreneurial self emerges through an ongoing process of becoming – an engagement with chance, contingency and creative responsiveness. Arguably, no other figure more fully embodies Friedrich Nietzsche's observation that in contemporary society we are beset by diverse, irreconcilable values, requiring each of us to set our own standards. The entrepreneur lives out this experimental existence, embracing uncertainty and 'becoming' through the act of venturing into the unknown, through proffering of alternatives, often oppositional ones. This insight invites deeper explorations of both how organizations are formed, and stakeholders are engaged in sustaining what we might call 'good shape' – a venture that remains dynamic yet coherent amidst uncertainty and change.

In bringing entrepreneurship and ethics into philosophical dialogue, each field can deepen its appreciation of itself and the other. Entrepreneurship studies can learn from how ethicists have conceptualized difference, authenticity, autonomy, duty, care and recognition. These ethical-philosophical concepts invite a deeper reflection on the responsibilities of entrepreneurs – not only towards stakeholders but towards the wider social and ecological systems in which they operate. In turn, ethical theorists can learn from entrepreneurship's philosophical examination of contingency, creativity, and emergent futures that foregrounds fluidity, moral luck, and improvisation.

Potential topics

  • Philosophical Dimensions of Ethics: How do different philosophical traditions (e.g., virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism, phenomenology, hermeneutics) inform our understanding of entrepreneurship as an ethical practice? How are traditions confirmed or transformed when ethics is viewed through an entrepreneurial lens?
  • Phenomenology of the Entrepreneurial Experience: In what sense are entrepreneurial experiences of uncertainty, autonomy, and decision-making ethical, and how does phenomenology illuminate Kierkegaard's 'finitude' of lived reality?
  • The Entrepreneur and Ethical Subjectivity: How can ethical theories of 'subjecthood', agency, embodiment, and 'self' inform understandings of the entrepreneur, and how might post-human ethics further enrich the question 'Who is the entrepreneur'?
  • Ethics and Rule-Breaking: Ethically, what is the connection between following and breaking rules, and how might entrepreneurial theory enrich understandings of this connection?
  • Stakeholder Relations and Trust: How do entrepreneurs navigate stakeholder dynamics and trust-building while pursuing ethical objectives and are these forms of trust akin to those envisaged in current ethical theorising?
  • Entrepreneurship as Inherently Ethical or Unethical: Is entrepreneurship inherently ethical or exploitative, and how can these views inform a more nuanced understanding of entrepreneurial ethics? How core are ethics to entrepreneurship?
  • Entrepreneurship and Technological Mediation: In the digital age of machine protocols, does judgment still matter—and is entrepreneurship a break from, or reinvention of, the network, platform, and stack?
  • Ethics, Value, and Entrepreneurial Goals: Can ethical theories of value and worth contribute to the framing of entrepreneurial goals and opportunity?
  • Temporal Dimensions of Entrepreneurial Ethics: How do entrepreneurial decisions compare immediate gains with long-term ethical considerations? In what ways does the entrepreneurial relationship to time create unique ethical challenges and opportunities?

Timeline

  • September 30, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: The Ethics of Gender Paradoxes in Organizations
item.content:encoded:
Pauline Reinecke, Leuphana University Lüneburg

Ignas Bruder, Technische Universität Dresden

Tobias Hahn, Esade Business School

Olga Kokshagina, University of Sydney

Stephanie Schrage, Kiel University

Janina Sundermeier, Freie Universität Berlin

Gender paradoxes emerge from tensions embedded in organizations, where competing expectations generate not only managerial challenges but also fundamental ethical questions about inclusion, equality, and responsibility. While prior research has examined barriers such as the glass ceiling and pay inequality, less attention has been paid to how gender paradoxes subtly yet systematically shape organizational experiences and allocate moral responsibilities among actors.

Gender is approached as an institutionalized system of social practices for constituting people as two significantly different categories, men and women, and organizing social relations of inequality on the basis of that difference. At the same time, the special issue recognizes the lived realities of intersex, non-binary, genderfluid, and other gender-diverse individuals who navigate structures grounded in binary norms.

Paradoxes, defined as contradictory yet interrelated elements that exist simultaneously and persist over time, are central to many tensions related to gender in organizations. These include the double bind women leaders face in balancing agentic and communal expectations, the difficulties gender-diverse individuals encounter when resisting dominant norms of professionalism, and the strain between care responsibilities and workplace demands for emotional detachment.

Gender paradoxes raise critical ethical questions: Whose interests are prioritized? Who bears moral and emotional burdens? What responsibilities do organizations, and specifically those organizational members unaffected by exclusion, hold in addressing these tensions? And when do such tensions call for institutional reform rather than individual adaptation? This Special Issue seeks to foreground the ethical dimensions of gender paradoxes in organizations.

The special issue welcomes original contributions that examine gender paradoxes not only analytically but also through ethically grounded normative arguments about how individuals and organizations can and should respond. Submissions should critically engage with ethical questions posed by gender paradoxes such as how moral responsibility is distributed, what burden visibility imposes, and how organizational actions with moral intent may reproduce inequality.

Submissions may tap into a range of theoretical traditions, including paradox, identity, institutional, practice, and discourse theory – as well as normative frameworks such as feminist ethics, ethics of care, virtue ethics, deontological approaches to ethics, and critical management studies. The special issue explicitly welcomes theoretically and methodologically diverse submissions that offer distinct insights into the empirical phenomenon of gender paradoxes, examining how related tensions are generated, navigated, and contested in organizational life.

Potential topics

  • Systemic constraints: How ethical commitments to inclusion and equality clash with organizational systems optimized for efficiency – such as standardized evaluations, established management practices, or masculinized leadership norms
  • Competing values and moral ambiguity: How ideals such as fairness, meritocracy, and equity create ethical tensions and "tragic choices", where no option is without compromise
  • Limits of both/and thinking: How both/and strategies for navigating gender paradoxes can foster more inclusive responses, but may also obscure structural inequalities and shift responsibility to individuals
  • Symbolic inclusion and tokenism: How efforts such as diversity targets or flexible work arrangements may produce ethically problematic outcomes, including constrained agency, limited advancement, and superficial change
  • Stigma, visibility, and marginalization: How gender-diverse professionals experience and resist stigmatization within organizations, raising ethical questions about who bears the burden of representation

Timeline

  • August 31, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: Animals and Business Ethics: Reimagining Multispecies Co-existence In Business and Society
item.content:encoded:
Doris Schneeberger, Vienna University of Economics and Business

Linda Tallberg, University of Lapland

José-Carlos García-Rosell, University of Oulu

Astrid Huopalainen, Aalto University

Eline Jammaers, Hasselt University

Katherine Dashper, Leeds Beckett University

Helen Wadham, Manchester Metropolitan University

Whilst human treatment of animals has long been a subject of considerable debate within the ethics literature, it is only in more recent years that scholars in business have examined ethical issues around the tourism and food industries, innovation, business education, animal rights and business failure, posthumanism, art, work involving animals, multispecies space, animal protection work, and stakeholder theory. Such interest is to be welcomed. Nevertheless, the interest that business scholars have shown in animals remains piecemeal, and often seems unaware of non-Western or indigenous perspectives. Additionally, ongoing technological developments that have the potential to radically transform the moral demarcations we make between humans and animals have hitherto received limited attention. Such transformations could slow down, or potentially reverse, the exponential increase in human domination over animals that has been evidenced over the past two centuries, and could significantly impact producers who still depend on traditional ways of animal production.

In light of such considerations, this special issue seeks studies that critically examine human-animal relations in the workplace, industry, or other societally organized spaces. Contributions should take an ethical, political, and/or multispecies lens to bring animals from the margins to the center of focus and analysis. The editors are especially interested in scholarly work that builds on interdisciplinary insights from animal ethics in general.

Industrial animal agriculture not only causes enormous animal suffering but also has severe negative ramifications for our planetary ecosystem, biodiversity, climate change, and species extinction. Despite this, meat production is at its highest level ever, with an expanding animal industry. The world consumption per capita of poultry, for instance, went from 10 to 15 kg in the period 2000-2019. Given that these animals are commonly raised in inhumane and unnatural circumstances, further discussion on the ethical challenges of killing sentient animals for food, and of alternative ways of producing animal products such as slaughter-free meat technology, is required.

Corporate disclosure concerning animal welfare also awaits further discussion. Companies may be reluctant to include animals in their CSR reports and codes of ethics, fearing potential accountability issues from powerful activists and social movements. Only a few recent scholarly efforts have explored the question of CSR and animal welfare. Some scholars have chosen to be deliberately critical and provoke change by, for example, advocating for an accounting of animal welfare as a potential avenue forward.

Recent work on DEI has highlighted the overlapping inequalities animals and marginalised humans face, requiring equality policies that are both multispecies and intersectional. Others too have called for more research around intersecting issues of asymmetrical power and care, like the ecofeminist tradition, as well as interspecies solidarity and justice. Developing multispecies inclusivity based on illuminating the animal's standpoint moves the traditional organizational lens to a post-anthropocentric way of perceiving, fostering multispecies wellbeing. Scholars might also seek inspiration from Indigenous ontologies which perceive life as interconnected.

Potential topics

  • Applying animal ethics theories to business ethics: Using specific animal ethics theories (e.g., rights-based, utilitarian, care ethics) to address business ethics issues
  • Corporate disclosure, CSR, and accounting for animals: Examining how businesses disclose and account for their impact on animals
  • Expanding business ethics frameworks to include animals: Discussing how stakeholder theory, corporate moral responsibility, or, for example, triple bottom line (TBL) approaches could incorporate animals
  • Non-Western and Indigenous ethical perspectives on multispecies organizations: Exploring how Indigenous and non-Western philosophies can inform business-ethics approaches to animals
  • Animals as workers: Investigating ethical concerns regarding animals used as workers in diverse settings, from agriculture to entertainment
  • Diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) and the role of animals: Extending DEI discussions to consider nonhuman animals in business contexts
  • Multispecies inclusivity: Analyzing how businesses can integrate multispecies perspectives into ethical and operational frameworks
  • Animal tourism: Addressing ethical challenges and exploitation in wildlife tourism, zoos, and entertainment industries
  • Technological innovations and their impact on animals: Examining cultivated animal products, alternative proteins, AI, and digitalization in relation to animals
  • Farmed animals and emerging business models: Investigating ethical issues in new farming methods such as precision and regenerative agriculture
  • Hard-to-access animal-use industries: Exploring ethical concerns in medical research, pharmaceuticals, and laboratory testing

Timeline

  • August 31, 2026: Submission deadline
